ancient.name: Khnum-Nakht
ancient.story_individual:
Khnum-Nakht was an ancient Egyptian priest during the 12th Dynasty who was buried in the Tomb of Two Brothers near modern-day Deir Rifeh, in the cemetery of the ancient town of Shashotep.

His brother was Nakht-Ankh. The two brothers are known only from their shared tomb. Khnum-Nakht held multiple titles including son of governor, son of the son of a governor and wab-priest of Khnum, lord of Shashotep. Archaeological evidence and later genetic analysis suggest that he and Nakht-Ankh were half-brothers who shared the same mother but had different fathers.

While researchers were unable to determine Khnum-Nakht's Y-DNA haplogroup, genetic analysis from the Drosou et al. 2018 study confirmed that he shared the mitochondrial haplogroup M1a1 with his brother Nakht-Ankh, supporting the theory that they had the same mother.

References

  • Drosou, K., Price, C., & Brown, T. A. (2018). The kinship of two 12th Dynasty mummies revealed by ancient DNA sequencing. Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports, 17, 793-797. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jasrep.2017.12.025

  • Price, C. (2023). Interpreting the 'Two Brothers' at Manchester Museum: Science, Knowledge and Display. Arch, 19, 104-128. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11759-023-09475-4

Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia.

ancient.name: Sima de los Huesos
ancient.story_individual:
Around 400,000 years ago, a hominin died and their remains ended up in what would become known as Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) in northern Spain. The individual's remains, including a femur which would later yield crucial DNA evidence, were preserved alongside approximately 28 other individuals in the cave system at Atapuerca. While researchers cannot determine this individual's biological sex, they know they belonged to a population that showed Neanderthal-like features in their skeletal morphology.

The remarkable preservation of their DNA was made possible by the stable, cold conditions within the cave. When the femur was analyzed in 2014, the DNA retrieved from it represented the oldest human DNA ever sequenced, pushing back the boundaries of ancient DNA research by hundreds of thousands of years. The mitochondrial DNA unexpectedly showed closer affinity to Denisovans than to Neanderthals, despite the skeletal characteristics of the population.

The recovery of such ancient DNA was a major technical achievement that required innovative methods to deal with highly degraded genetic material. While we don't know the details of this individual's life - what they ate, how they lived, or how they died - their genetic legacy has provided crucial insights into human evolution and the complex relationships between ancient hominin populations.

Subsequent nuclear DNA analysis of Sima de los Huesos hominins revealed a closer connection to Neanderthals than the mtDNA initially suggested, adding another fascinating layer to this individual's story.

References

  • Meyer, M., Fu, Q., Aximu-Petri, A. et al. A mitochondrial genome sequence of a hominin from Sima de los Huesos. Nature 505, 403–406 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12788

  • Meyer, M., Arsuaga, JL., de Filippo, C. et al. Nuclear DNA sequences from the Middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos hominins. Nature 531, 504–507 (2016). https://doi.org/10.1038/nature17405

Pictured: Cranium 17 of the Sima de los Huesos, from an individual from the same location and time period. Nohemi Sala, Juan Luis Arsuaga, Ana Pantoja-Pérez, Adrián Pablos, Ignacio Martínez, Rolf M. Quam, Asier Gómez-Olivencia, José María Bermúdez de Castro, Eudald Carbonell, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Robert Siegel
famous.story_individual:
Robert Siegel is a distinguished American journalist and broadcaster, best known for his three-decade tenure as host of NPR's flagship program "All Things Considered." His journey in journalism began during his student years at Columbia University, where he served as an anchor covering the 1968 Columbia demonstrations for the college radio station WKCR-FM. He graduated from Columbia College that same year and spent a year at Columbia's Graduate School of Journalism.

Siegel's career at NPR was marked by several pioneering achievements. In 1979, he became NPR's first overseas-based staff member, reporting from London until 1983. Upon returning to the United States, he took on a leadership role as director of the News and Information Department, where he oversaw the production of both "All Things Considered" and "Morning Edition," while also helping launch "Weekend Edition." In 1987, Siegel began his most well-known role as host of "All Things Considered," a position he would hold until his retirement in 2018, with a brief interlude in 1992 to host NPR's call-in show "Talk of the Nation."

His excellence in journalism was recognized with the prestigious John Chancellor Award from Columbia University's Graduate School of Journalism in 2010. Beyond radio, Siegel made his mark in popular culture through cameo appearances in several television shows, including "The Simpsons," "Northern Exposure," and "BoJack Horseman," as well as the film "Yesterday Was a Lie." Throughout his career, he became known for his thoughtful interviewing style and clear, authoritative delivery of news stories.

His mtDNA haplogroup was revealed in the 2012 September-October issue of Moment Magazine.

famous.name: Liangdao Man
famous.story_individual:
Liangdao Man was an individual who lived approximately 8,300 years ago on what is now Liang Island (also called Larne Island), a small island in the Taiwan Strait located about 24 kilometers offshore from Fujian, China. This person was part of a coastal population that lived during the early Neolithic period in Southeast Asia.

The skeleton was discovered in December 2011 on Liang Island, which today is part of Taiwan's Matsu Islands. Genetic analysis revealed that Liangdao Man carried specific maternal DNA (mitochondrial Haplogroup E) and paternal DNA (Y-chromosome Haplogroup O-M119, subclade O-CTS5726) that provides important insights into early human populations in the region.

The individual's genetic profile suggests they were part of a southern ancestry group that inhabited the coastal areas of mainland southern China and the Taiwan Strait islands. This ancestry continues today most prominently in Austronesian-speaking peoples across Taiwan and Maritime Southeast Asia.

The location and time period of Liangdao Man suggest they were likely a maritime-adapted person, living on a small island and presumably engaging in fishing and seafaring activities, though we don't have direct evidence of their specific lifestyle. Their remains have become crucial evidence in understanding early human migration patterns and the ancestry of modern East Asian populations.

References

  • Larena, M., Sjödin, P., McKenna, J., Ebeo, C., Reyes, R., Casel, O., Huang, J., Hagada, K. P., Guilay, D., Reyes, J., Allian, F. P., Mori, V., Azarcon, L. S., Manera, A., Terando, C., Jamero, L., Sireg, G., Labos, M. S., Vilar, R. D., . . . Jakobsson, M. (2021). Multiple migrations to the Philippines during the last 50,000 years. famous.name: Señora de Cao
famous.story_individual:
The Lady of Cao was a high-ranking Moche woman who lived in Peru's Chicama Valley around 500 CE. She died in her mid-to-late 20s and was discovered in 2006 at the Huaca Cao Viejo archaeological site.

Recent genetic analysis reveals she was part of an elite family, with at least one brother and likely another sibling, plus a grandfather also buried nearby. She received the most elaborate burial of her family group, suggesting she held the highest status.

Her well-preserved mummy shows extensive tattoos of spiders and snakes. She was buried with symbols of both male and female power: ceremonial weapons (spear-throwers and clubs) alongside gold crowns and nose ornaments. A young female relative was sacrificed to accompany her in death.

The Lady of Cao's discovery challenged previous assumptions that only men held high positions in Moche society. Her burial predates other known female Moche priestesses by about 200 years, making her one of the earliest documented female rulers in ancient Peru.

Reconstruction model showing the Lady of Cao wearing ceremonial garments and holding ritual staffs, based on burial artifacts and forensic facial modeling. Jean-Pierre Dalbéra from Paris, France, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Her body was carefully preserved with seawater and cinnabar, allowing her tattoos and other features to remain visible 1,500 years later. In 2017, researchers created a facial reconstruction using 3D imaging technology, providing a glimpse of her appearance.

References

  • Quilter, J., Harkins, K., Fanco Jordan, R., Marsh, E., Prieto, G., Verano, J., LeBlanc, S., Broomandkhoshbacht, N., & Krigbaum, J. (2025). Family relations of Moche elite burials on the North Coast of Peru (~500 CE): Analyses of the Señora de Cao and relatives. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 122(1), e2416321121. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2416321121

Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Korguz
famous.story_individual:
The Shuzhuanglou site in the Hebei province of China was found to contain 13 skeletons, 6 men and 7 women, in six different tombs. The archaeological evidence indicates that the cemetery occupants were Mongol nobles and dates the burial site to the Yuan Dynasty (1271-1368 CE).

Evidence strongly suggests that the man from the main tomb was Korguz, the fifth chief of the Ongüd tribe, which was a Turkic tribe who later became Mongols and were allies of Kublai Khan.

The Shuzhuanglou building above ground (黑夜有灯, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The chief occupant, a man who was around 40, was buried in the main tomb with two women. An inscription found in his tomb says Korguz (Chinese: 阔里吉斯), and it is thought to be the name of the tomb occupant. A coin from the Yuan Dynasty dated to 1310-1311 CE was also found in his tomb and provides the earliest date of burial. His mtDNA haplogroup was determined to be D4m2.

Korguz (not to be confused with Uyghur Korguz who died in 1242) was the fifth chief of the Ongüd tribe, descending from the Tūjué (突厥), also known as the Göktürks. Historical records say that he married Kublai Khan’s two granddaughters and fought against Kaidu, the great-grandson of Genghis Khan. He was captured and killed in 1298 and reburied by his son in 1311, matching the date of the coin. The two women buried in the main tomb could be the Mongol princesses.

Three of the men, including the chief occupant, were DNA tested by Y. Cui et al. 2015, and all were found to belong to Y-DNA haplogroup Q. No further testing for more specific Y-DNA haplogroups was performed.

Information sourced from Yinqiu Cui et al. 2015, “Identification of kinship and occupant status in Mongolian noble burials of the Yuan Dynasty through a multidisciplinary approach.”

Pictured: A "Zhida Tongbao" (至大通寶) coin issued under Külüg Khan, same as found in the tomb. Jean-Michel Moullec from Vern sur Seiche (35, Bretagne), France, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

famous.name: At Daban 6 Woman
famous.story_individual:
The At Daban 6 Woman, an 18th-century figure from Siberia, was a high-status individual buried at the At Daban site, 2 km from the Istiakh terrace. Her grave, richly adorned with two Russian signet rings (heraldic and hagiographic), lobed enamel buttons, and a dagger from Velikiy Ustiug, reflects her significant social standing and connections to Russian trade networks. Genetic analysis reveals her mitochondrial DNA haplogroup as D5a2a, linking her maternal lineage to East Asian populations, particularly prevalent among groups like the Yakuts in Central and Northeast Asia. DNA evidence confirms she was the mother of an adult male buried 2.5 km away at Sytygane Syhé 1, dated to 1700–1750. Her ties to the Y-DNA Ht1 lineage, associated with Mazary Bozekov, suggest she belonged to a prominent family, possibly with political influence in the region.

At Daban 6 grave goods and reconstructed dress with a large number of imported glass beads. Zvénigorosky et al. 2020, Fig. 3 (cropped), CC-BY-4.0.

famous.name: Joshua Bell
famous.story_individual:
Joshua Bell is one of America's most celebrated classical violinists, first gaining attention as a child prodigy when he performed with the Philadelphia Orchestra at age 14. He was named Music Director of the Academy of St Martin in the Fields in 2011, becoming the first person to hold this position since Sir Neville Marriner founded the orchestra.

Bell is known for playing the Gibson ex-Huberman Stradivarius violin from 1713, valued at around $4 million. This instrument has a remarkable history - it was stolen twice from its previous owner, Bronisław Huberman. Bell purchased it in 2001.

A notable moment in Bell's career came from an experiment with The Washington Post in 2007. He performed incognito as a street musician in a DC Metro station during rush hour. Despite being one of the world's finest violinists, he earned only $32.17 from rushing commuters, demonstrating how context affects the perception of art. This experiment won the Post a Pulitzer Prize.

Bell continues to perform worldwide and has recorded over 40 albums, winning multiple Grammy Awards. He frequently collaborates across genres, working with artists like Josh Groban and Chick Corea, and has appeared on numerous television shows including The Tonight Show and Dancing with the Stars.

His mtDNA haplogroup was revealed in the 2012 September-October issue of Moment Magazine.

Pictured: By Alexduff - Own work, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. Biography in part generated using Anthropic (2025) Claude 3.5 Sonnet [Large language model].

famous.name: Margaret Cho
famous.story_individual:
Margaret Cho is a comedian, actress, and musician. She started her stand-up comedy career at age 14, and as a young teenager, won a contest to open for Jerry Seinfeld and had appearances on The Arsenio Hall Show and in a Bob Hope special.

Cho is the daughter of Korean immigrants. On Finding Your Roots, it was revealed that her paternal grandfather was a Christian minister working for the Japanese during their occupation of Korea during World War II. He was labeled a traitor, and her grandparents and father, who was a small child at the time, fled to South Korea.

In 1964, Cho’s parents immigrated to America and settled in San Francisco, where she was raised. Cho’s stand-up routine often focuses on the conflict between traditional Korean and American culture, which she struggled with growing up in the Castro district.

Cho starred in a sitcom based on her stand-up routine, All-American Girl, from 1994 to 1995. She was part of the main cast of the television series Drop Dead Diva, held a starring role in Fire Island, and was nominated for an Emmy for Outstanding Guest Actress in a Comedy Series for her appearance on 30 Rock impersonating Kim Jong-Il. In 2017, Rolling Stone magazine named her one of the top 50 stand-up comics.

Cho is an outspoken political advocate for LGBTQi+ issues and has received awards from the Gay and Lesbian Alliance Against Defamation (GLAAD), Lambda Legal, the National Organization for Women (NOW), and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU).

Margaret Cho’s mtDNA haplogroup was revealed on Finding Your Roots season 1 episode 8. Biographical information sourced from Wikipedia and Finding Your Roots. Pictured: Margaret Cho performing at Jesse Hall, KOMUnews, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

famous.name: Kristi Yamaguchi
famous.story_individual:
Olympic figure skating champion, Kristine “Kristi” Yamaguchi brought home the gold in 1992, the first Asian American woman to do so.

By Cliff from Arlington, VA (Outside Washington DC), USA - Kristi Yamaguchi’s Figure Skates, 1990’s, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia

Kristi excelled on the ice rink, winning two World figure skating championships in 1991 and 1992 in spite of having been born with bi-lateral club foot, resulting in her legs being in casts for most of the first year of her life.

Born in California, Kristi’s father was a dentist and tested his Y-DNA for the Faces of America PBS series hosted by Henry Louis Gates, Jr. His parents immigrated to the United States from Japan.

Yamaguchi’s grandfather, Tatsuichi Yamaguchi arrived in Hawaii in 1899. Gates indicated that his heritage reached back to Wakayama and Saga prefectures in Japan and that about 20% of the people in Japan are very distant cousins.

Sourced from: Faces of America book by Henry Louis Gates, Jr., Wikipedia, and Olympics.com.

famous.name: Neanderthal Man
famous.story_individual:
Neanderthals were first named and unearthed in 1856 in the Neander Valley of Germany, three full years before Darwin published his book On the Origin of Species. In his writings, Darwin only briefly wrote about human evolution and did not mention anything about the newly named Neanderthals. Coincidentally, by 1848, a Neanderthal skeleton had already been discovered in Gibraltar. That specimen, however, had remained uncharacterized in science. So, as fate would have it, the German team is credited with discovering the new species, and the name Neanderthal still remains. Neanderthal Man (seen pictured as a reconstruction) from Feldhofer cave in Neander Valley lived approximately 40,000 years ago.

Today, we know much more about these cousins of Homo sapiens (humans), when and where they lived and how they may have mated with our stone-age ancestors. In 2008, a team led by Nobel Laureate Svante Pääbo sequenced the first Neanderthal genome, and just months after that publication, anthropologists discovered that Neanderthal DNA still resided in most humans alive today. Yes, humans and Neanderthals had mated.

Although the common evolutionary ancestor to Homo sapiens and Neanderthals lived more than half-a-million years ago, we now know that the Y chromosome of the male Neanderthals sequenced to date came from an introduction event (a mating) between a male archaic human and a female Neanderthal between 370,000 and 100,000 years ago. This, and other new findings, suggests that mixing between human ancestors and Neanderthals occurred early and possibly frequently while they co-existed for millennia in Europe and Asia, which was until approximately 35,000 years ago when Neanderthals went extinct. 

We are fortunate to be living in an amazing time where every year new discoveries add exciting information about humans, our ancestors, and our shared prehistory. The last decade alone has completely reshaped our knowledge and relationship with the once mighty Neanderthals.

Homo neanderthalensis reconstruction - Mr. N

©Neanderthal Museum

The divergence time between modern human and Neanderthal Y chromosomes was estimated by Petr et al. 2020. The evolutionary history of Neanderthal and Denisovan Y chromosomes. The A000-T haplogroup name comes from the ISOGG Y-DNA Haplogroup Tree 2019-2020.
